newsitem.title: NEPAL: FEATURE-Nepal looks between mountains for tourism.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Nepal looks between mountains for tourism.

text.p: Officials in Nepal plan to look for new tourist attractions among the Himalayan kingdom's snow-capped peaks, which have lured thousands of mountaineers and trekkers annually for decades.
Tourism officials plan to promote the ancient kingdom's cultural heritage and traditional Nepali activities repackaged as new adventure sports.

Mountaineering and trekking have been the cornerstone of tourism, Nepal's largest source of foreign exchange after foreign aid. Eight of the world's 14 tallest peaks, including Mount Everest, are in Nepal.

But hotel owners complain that room occupancy dips below 50 percent from December to February in the Himalayan winter and in the rainy season that lasts from July to September. Nepal has about 7,000 hotel rooms.
MISSION: 500,000 VISITORS
"We have not been able to change from traditional tourism," said hotel owner Karna Shakya, referring to mountaineering and trekking.
In 1995, 363,000 tourists visited Nepal, bringing in $117 million -- four percent of the kingdom's gross domestic product. More than 85,000 visitors were trekkers or mountain-climbers.

Authorities say their target is to attract half a million tourists in 1998. The kingdom draws more than 100,000 honeymooners and shoppers every year from neighbouring India. They pay as little as $150 for a return ticket to Kathmandu -- about half the air fare between New Delhi and Bombay.

Indian nationals, who account for well over one-third of Nepal's tourists, need neither a passport nor a visa to visit Nepal, often travelling by road across the common border. Both nations' airlines fly daily between Kathmandu and five Indian cities.
Nepali tour operators are now urging Kathmandu to ask India to allow private flights between three towns in Nepal and three cities in northern India.

Shakya, who is coordinating a "Visit Nepal Year 1998" campaign, told Reuters the government planned to cater to foreign visitors' thirst for adventure by promoting traditional Nepali activities as new adventure sports.

Visitors can now participate in such activities as honey hunting in central Nepal, where villagers dangle from ropes tied round their their waists on windswept cliffs to extract honey from the hives of wild bees.
"It is an exciting and romantic way in which to attract tourists," Shakya said.
FRESH FOCUS ON RELIGION AND WILDLIFE
Officials say they also plan to market the world's only Hindu kingdom as the home of Buddhist shrines and one of Hinduism's most sacred shrines, the Pashupatinath temple.
Nepal has more than 1,000 Buddhist monasteries, including the Swyambhunath and Boudhnath stupas, ancient Buddhist monuments that are among the seven world heritage sites in the country.
Although only Hindus are allowed to visit the Pashupatinath temple, all tourists are permitted in other Hindu shrines.
Wildlife lovers are already flocking to southern Nepal's Royal Chitaun national park, one of the two places in the world with more than 300 great Asian one-horned rhinoceroses.
Chitaun is also the world's only venue for elephant polo, and is popular among Western tourists who can watch royal Bengal tigers while riding an elephant.
Officials say the new tourism campaign is focused on India and newly affluent consumers in southeast Asia.
ETIQUETTE DRIVE
Nearly half of Nepal's visitors come from Asia. West European travellers currently account for more than a third of the kingdom's tourists.
In a drive to help Nepalis deal with foreign visitors, the Tourism Ministry has distributed a pamphlet on etiquette in 4,000 villages.
"Don't shake hands with a woman tourist unless she gives her hand first to you," the booklet says.
"Don't spit when tourists are near and when they come to your premises, be polite and offer them a seat."
